text:
I think the saying "Misery loves company", applies to a lot of post here

I am a long time lurker in this sub and I constantly read stories from professionals and students struggling to find work and I certainly agree with them, but there is more to it. To briefly describe my own story I applied to hundreds of jobs after graduating with my BS and only managed to find a contract role doing mostly IT work and then I was eventually laid off after 2 years. I then found my first software engineering role about 7 months ago after job searching again for 6 months and frankly I was only able to get this role by finally reaching outside of my bubble and asking everyone I knew for help in the job search, friends, family, and former peers I worked on projects with. Even when I secured this role, I had to leave everything behind, my friends, my family, and my hometown to move across the country for it. I am still trying to break into something that will allow me to return home even though I am paid well and get great benefits. 
 I don't say this to brag, but to give others hope and ideas, sometimes you have to take a suboptimal path if it gives you time in today's market. I worked as an IT Support for 2 years while being underpaid because it was my only option. For me and I'm sure many of you, there was never any other choice than CS, I see many others warning new grads and perspective students not to pursue CS, but if its the only path you can see yourself doing it doesn't make sense to do anything else and live a life of regret. I remember when I first started CS and my professor in my C++ 101 class warned everyone that in this field everything is constantly changing and to choose CS is to more so than other majors, make a commitment to life-long learning and constant adaptability.
 To wrap this up, I am quite young in my career and I expect to get laid off soon always now and have learned you should never put trust in one company no matter how secure they may seem, build an emergency fund, and keep your resume and skill-set updated. For students still in college the single best advice I can give is try to talk to everyone, join sports, clubs, college parties, whatever you need to do to meet more people, increase your communication skills and have a higher chance of meeting someone who can get you a job, in my opinion this is the highest return activity in college even beyond getting a good GPA and an area where I focused on the wrong things. For graduates seeking to find employment my advice is the same, talk to everyone you can and don't suffer in silence alone while rapid-firing thousands of applications to the LinkedIn and Indeed void for an AI to automatically reject, while your parents and friends tell you, you aren't trying hard enough. Its funny that I find myself sounding like a War Veteran after going through so much trouble and rejection and I'm still so young in my career. My hope is that this post at least helps one person and things get better. Good luck.

text:
A realistic,”mid” career

Warning: long story. 
 I’m employed but not in FAANG or “high” finance so I thought I’d share my story as opposed to all the unemployed doomers and/or people bragging about huge salaries/TC.
 I spent my late teens and early 20s f-ing around at random dead end jobs and playing MMOs.
 Eventually I graduated from a no name public state rural college with a BS in CS. Afterwards I got a programming job relatively fast (this was the late 2010s) about a month post graduation at a local it consultancy that specialized in peoplesoft but the side of the company I worked on developed a custom app for the state government that was written in Java (albeit a “heavyweight” old school niche enterprise stack). After that I got bored of my job so I decided to go to grad school full time online during the pandemic at a private midwestern college for a masters and graduate just before ChatGPT blew up.
 After that I was unemployed for months as I lived in a very different time zone from most of the companies I was applying to so doing interviews required me to either stay up to the early morning or wake up early (like 3-5 am). Because of that I bombed a lot of interviews as this is not exactly a good state of mind to try and solve algorithmic interview problems plus during the day I couldn’t really sleep as my parents wanted me to go do things in town with them and we didn’t have aircon anyway so id just be sweating and not sleeping anyway (even with a junior dev salary at the first job I still lived with my parents as this was a VHCOL area)
 Anyway after a few months of that my only job offer was a body shop consultancy with an exploitative contract which forced you to pay tens of thousands of dollars if you quit early. I was “trained” as a Java/SQL dev (which I already knew so it was easy) and placed at a company as a “devops” engineer but more accurately it was as a production support analyst debugging batch jobs and supporting overnight processing. Eventually I ended up using my coding skills to automate parts of the job which led to me getting internally assigned to moonlight as a python dev rewriting financial risk models made by the quants from janky desktop tools into “real” production software with unit tests and linting and database integration etc. eventually getting to work on CI/CD and more traditionally devopsy things.
 Right now the company is going through a cloud rewrite of their main software which is changing us from on prem and mainframe to cloud and kubernetes, also heavily Kafka/flink based, so I’m studying for certifications in those areas to upgrade my skills. The current plan is to merge legacy production support into the cloud devops team once the new system goes live - or maybe I’ll just be laid off, who knows. 
 My compensation timeline ->
 HR TECH consultancy - $60k in VHCOL, no bonuses, 401k matching took 12 years to vest
 Body shop -$45k (2 years contract to hire)
 Finance place - $85k and 8-10% bonus
 Promoted at finance place - $104k base and same bonus.
 So right now I make about $104k a year and I have about 6 YOE not counting the 2 years doing my masters. It’s very stressful because even in a MCOL location I barely have enough money to pay rent and groceries because I’m also paying my student loans and supporting my girlfriend who has been unemployed for a year and a half.  Overall approach - Plan the following changes and ask any clarifying questions if needed. Generate a few test cases that include edge cases, and troubleshoot the approach against these cases. We will be using a dictionary with a doubly linked list to achieve all the operations in constant time. Structure of the Doubly linked list - Prev next pointers as standard. The val field would be an array/set of strings + an integer (frequency). Each node would be a bucket for a frequency. If 5 words appear 5 times, then a node with value would have those 5 strings in it's set. Dictionary design - Simple key -> value where key is a string, and value is the node in which string is present. (Here node means the bucket. So if the bucket's val's set contains that string -> the mapping b/w key and value should exist. Instructions - Init - Just instantiate the dictionary and the DLL. Inc - Check if the value is already present. If YES, get the node. Check the adjacent node (to the right). If it has a frequency of old value + 1, then move the string from the current bucket to the next bucket. If NO, create a new bucket (node) and insert to right. Dec - Check if the value is already present. If YES, get the node. Check the adjacent node (to the left). If it has a frequency of old value - 1, then move the string from the current bucket to the previous bucket. If NO, create a new bucket (node) and insert to left. If this is the first element being added, you would have to create a new node, and set the head and tail to it. Get max key - Return a random value from the tail Get min key - Return a random value from the head. The DLL is basically a sorted list of frequency buckets. Encouraged to ask questions before starting implementation to ensure correctness. Stress test the cases against the problem statement and expected output.  Would something like this pass the bar? text:
After 22 years in IT, I can tell you AI is not replacing developers. It's replacing syntax coding

I remember in the early 2000s reading a book called "My Job Went to India and All I Got Was This Lousy Book."
 On the cover, the author, Chad Fowler, had an Indian guy holding a sign that read, "Will code for food."
 Fowler described how software development jobs were moving to India at the time, and the challenges people in the US were facing with that transition: time zones, language barriers, cultural differences, and communication bottlenecks.
 We are in the exact same situation today with AI.
 If there is one thing AI is very good at, it is writing code. It can generate thousands of lines of syntax in seconds. Generating code has never been easier.
 But one of Fowler's core arguments, in a book that is now almost 20 years old, was that outsourcing syntax writing to entities who do not understand the architecture, the design, and the culture of the organization creates a set of secondary challenges.
 Writing software is not just churning out syntax. It requires a mental model and a deep understanding of what you are actually building.
 The exact same rule applies to AI agents.
 If you simply prompt an AI agent to build something without giving it a clear architecture, specific requirements, and deterministic guardrails, the agent will probably produce something. But who knows what you have actually built?
 It is not surprising that people who "vibe code" entire projects often either fail to finish them or abandon them completely because the codebase becomes impossible to maintain. That is the ultimate trap of vibe coding: maintainability.
 So yes, AI will write more and more of the code from now on. That code will become cheaper and cheaper to produce.
 But what will not go away, and what will actually become significantly more valuable, is the person who knows how to build systems structurally. The person who understands the architecture. The person who can see the entire system in their head before asking the AI to build it.
 AI is replacing the person writing the syntax. I am not convinced it will ever replace the person who knows what should be built in the first place.

text:
My entire software development workflow is AI now, and it feels both exhausting and soulless

I've been a SWE for a little over 4 years, and Claude has basically been a permanent coworker for the last year.
 At first, it was great. I already knew ChatGPT and Cursor, so when my team got Claude I adapted quickly and ended up way ahead of most of my coworkers in how I used it. I even got a significant raise partly because of that.
 Claude did a lot of the coding, but I was still doing the engineering. I understood the system, made the decisions, reviewed the output, and almost never shipped bugs or regressions.
 Now I'm just tired of LLMs, at least professionally.
 The tools got so good, and I've built so many skills, MCPs and docs around them, that a lot of my job is basically: tell Claude to read the project .md, read the ticket, press enter.
 And because everyone has access to the same tools now, productivity expectations exploded.
 Sprints that used to have 5 big tasks or 10 smaller ones now have several times that workload. We're expected to run multiple Claude instances in parallel and constantly multitask. Proper testing and engineering discussions have increasingly been replaced by automated tests, MCPs that can test on screen, and a "quantity over quality" approach.
 The weirdest part is that AI has taken over communication too.
 POs can feed client requirements into an internal Claude MCP connected to Azure, which outputs a task already tailored to the codebase. The SWE gives that task to Claude, Claude writes the code, automated tests find problems, and another AI generated message tells the SWE what failed.
 You ask someone a question, they send it to their AI, send the answer back to you, and then you send their answer to your AI.
 Everyone has this little AI parrot on their shoulder rewriting everything into the same sterile corporate language.
 I miss calling a PO and actually trying to understand a problem. I miss sitting with another engineer and debugging some horrible production issue together. I miss people actually knowing the systems they work on and sharing that knowledge.
 Now I barely feel familiar with most of the things I ship.
 When I get praised at work, I feel like an impostor. It doesn't feel like I built something. It feels like I gave experienced instructions to a magic shell that built it for me.
 I'm currently thinking about starting some kind of side business selling physical products. Maybe it'll fail, but at least I'd be learning something new, solving unfamiliar problems and actually exercising my brain again.
 I never thought I'd miss staying up all night fixing a critical bug or obsessively working on a personal project, but well, here we are.
 Fun fact: the original draft of this post was clumsy and too long, so what did I do? You probably know it by now. Sorry, but I just can't help it, and I guess it's how most people who work with LLMs feel right now.

text:
Advice Request/Discussion/Slight Vent regarding State of Software Development and Potential Steps Towards Pivoting Away from It

Apologies if this is redundant, as I'm sure there's a significant number of posts, articles, and other things near exactly like portions of this, but none seem to be an all-encompassing "walkthrough" of sorts about this as of yet, so I was curious to run it by everyone and gather opinions. Additional apologies for what I can only assume with result in being an essay-long post as I write this lol. After writing this all, I figure I'll attempt to break it into sections for those who don't want to read everything (although now it, ironically given the topic, borderline look AI generated... oh well)
 Essentially, as the title implies, I'm curious to try to sort of simultaneously summate opinions, gather advice towards future steps (either specialization or pivoting away from the field), verify info I've gathered, and additionally vent a little bit/voice my experience in the software field thus far. While some of these topics sort of brush against slightly political or charged topics, I hoping not to devolve the discussion into just those topics or to spark anything heated
 My Background/Partial Vent
 Mostly for context, but also to lead into the next portions, my background is about 6 years of software engineering at this point, with an additional partly completed masters degree. It's been a very rocky journey though (although I very much know this is not unique to me). Covid delayed me getting my first career job by almost a full year, and I had to accept the first one I was offered, which required moving to a very expensive location with very, very low pay. The company was great, despite this, but I eventually had to leave due to costs rising beyond what I could afford in that location. On top of applying to other jobs throughout the duration of the aforementioned one, it required almost a full additional year outside of it to land my next job. This required probably 4000+ applications in total due to a lack of experience at the time, most jobs shifting away from the experience I had gained, and the simultaneous extreme push to outsource employees at the time. This next job I landed at is, just like the first, an amazing company, but it offers no benefits, the pay is (in my opinion) a little low relative to the amount of experience I have. The pay, while objectively not bad, is also a lower number than I was hoping to make by this point in time when I started my career, and that was prior to the sharp inflation we've experienced since. There's also no real way to move up the company, and raises do not match the standard 3% increase schedule (made worse by individual health insurance costs skyrocketing on top of inflation)
 My experience started primarily with web development, but then shifted at first partly and then fully into desktop apps across two companies. By sheer chance, my "specialty" ended up becoming adapting very legacy code into either completely new project rebuilds or significant overhauls to allow for new software packages. Somehow, these also have always been in live environments, so changes matter, and testing is very limited. The code is so legacy that no documentation exists at all for the old software packages, which seems to render AI completely unable to make the necessary revisions even close to correctly (I'm assuming due to lack of training data?), and the live environment's requirements for precision make widespread changes by something like AI tricky. This has, ironically, completely removed me from the more "traditional" development spaces that seem to be seeing all the changes due to AI, especially as I have always somehow been put in charge of heading these rebuilds solely by myself. Even my current employer, as a company, has fully embraced AI as a tool, but I have managed to never use it to any significant degree, and thus I'm not personally sure about how it's impacting things beyond what I read
 The Current State of Software
 As mentioned previously, I'm a little more divorced from the overall current state of things than the average software developer, both due to the specific work I've been doing and the small companies I've exclusively worked with thus far. This makes it very, very hard for me to get a proper read on the trajectory of things, especially when it comes to this whole AI advancement thing that's been happening. One day I wake up and there's some new thing that ChatGPT is being famed for doing, only for it to turn out to be far less impressive than advertised the day after. The next day an AI coding agent destroys a company by screwing up its code. The day after, another new thing happened. Etc. I've seen mixes of posts on here saying that, while AI hasn't replaced their jobs, their jobs have devolved solely into writing prompts, hitting the submit button, and praying that the slot machine pays out properly this time around, as they aren't even allowed to manually modify the code anymore. Others say that their company has rejected AI entirely beyond basic revisions. Then I switch over to this sub and see studies pointing out that AI implementations, surprisingly, don't increase the overall throughput of companies due to many factors. Then in the replies of that and in other posts, people say that their companies have essentially swapped to being run fully by AI, and they're just sort of... there (which unfortunately seems to be the direction my company is heading). Then you have the Bureau of Labor Statistics still projecting an increase in job growth for software despite everything (although idk how accurate these projections have been, historically)
 Ramblings aside, I guess I'm just overall curious if there's a pulse on how future proof software development as a whole is, regardless of the form it takes. That is, while I'm not certain how long the big AI companies will stick around due to a significant number of factors, I have a striking feeling that, at minimum, local AI usage will remain as a consistent tool used in writing software pretty much indefinitely. Is this something that you all feel will remain a rather consistent gig, but now you just are expected to use AI tools, no different than moving from a low-level to high-level language as took place many years ago? Do you feel like this is something that, given time and ironing out of the issues, could potentially significantly threaten the career field? Do you think it'll just die out entirely for any reason, and it's just the temporary "new, current thing"?
 I guess my overall hesitancy is that, as I've seen many others voice, it seems like the current state of software engineering is no longer... engineering. I'm not at all opposed to learning new tools, but it seems like it's become, literally, just software development. As in, you no longer solve problems, engineer solutions, or try to optimize code (which I find myself doing any time I have AI output code; it's often horrendously optimized). You just sort of output it, which is not what I enjoy in the field. You almost act more as a manager of someone else creating the code, as a head software developer would manage an intern, but without writing the code yourself. Is this accurate as a whole?
 Moving into the Future
 In addition to the above, I guess I was also just curious what the future plans of everyone are. Are a significant number of you planning to jump ship, or do you plan to double down and see this through? Quite frankly, I've become significantly burned out on the insane back-and-forths of the career area since I've joined, where it seems like every company's #1 priority is the complete replacement of their software engineers for some reason, so I'm heavily debating what to do next. When I first started studying for this back in high school, this was supposed to be a very steady field, but the reality since has been very different, and the compensation, in my experience, has lagged significantly even without the constant threat of replacement and difficulty finding the jobs being a factor. That being said, I do believe I can have a steady future at my current company. That is, with them being a small company, they prefer to work with their employees and train them up rather than replace them. However, as mentioned prior, inflation is essentially guaranteed to outpace the pay over time (which I know doesn't make me unique in this instance, as everyone's suffering the same, but mine will be faster lol)
 An additional concern is that, if I were to swap career areas, I would be starting from scratch in a very unforgiving time frame. If I recall correctly, the average salary in every state in the US is below the average cost of living, and I'd be well below the average just starting out again. Even living in a cheap state and a small town, where expenses are lesser, I don't think any jobs I could get in the surrounding 30 mile radius could match the cost of even my basic expenses. That being said, are there any related career areas that might be more future proof that could be considerable to pivot to? That is, ones where you wouldn't necessarily be starting out from scratch, and while the pay might take a dip, it wouldn't plummet to starting-over-levels? Is it worth it to pursue education in something like cybersecurity or network infrastructure, which might outlast software? Would it be best that I just stay in my position, which again is by no means bad, and just accept that that's how it is and switching would just make things worse/more unstable?
 If there are no other real options to pivot to, what are some other things you're considering switching entirely to? Is the current state of software such that considering all of this isn't even worth it at this time?
 Thank you all for your time in reading this far, and for the advice!

text:
It's not just doomerism AI is fundamentally changing the job market for software engineers.

​
 Hi everyone, I've noticed that there are very different opinions about AI here. In my opinion, many people underestimate how much AI is already affecting the job market for software engineers and how many jobs could disappear in the long run.
 The logic is pretty simple: If developers become significantly more productive thanks to AI, companies need fewer people to build the same amount of software. So the real question is whether this increased productivity will create enough additional demand to offset the loss of jobs.
 This is where people often bring up the Jevons paradox as a counterargument: If software becomes cheaper to develop, more software will be built, potentially creating even more jobs.
 The problem with this argument is that demand for software isn't unlimited. Most companies develop software to solve specific problems. If an application needs 120 features, there's no economic reason to suddenly build 400 just because development has become cheaper. At some point, the product is simply finished, or at least good enough to serve its purpose.
 Of course, there are areas where the Jevons paradox could have a much stronger effect. For example, game development, embedded systems, or hardware development, where many ideas previously couldn't be realized because of high costs or limited engineering capacity.
 However, I don't believe the additional demand in these areas will be enough to compensate for the decline in traditional software engineering jobs.
 My prediction is that 50 to 80% of today's software engineering positions could eventually disappear. Not because software will no longer be needed, but because far fewer people will be required to develop and maintain it.
 As a result, I suspect many computer science graduates and software engineers will eventually have to move into other fields where human judgment, responsibility, and direct interaction with the physical world remain valuable advantages.

Even Andrew Ng is saying overhyped AI is causing harm and that CS degree will still be useful for decades to come

Thought it’d be useful for those in this field who are worried about the impact of AI on their careers, especially new grads and prospective CS students, to read this post by Andrew Ng (prominent ML/DL expert who confounded Google Brian and Coursera) on the harm of overhyping AI.
 TL;DR Frontier model progress is incredible especially how much it can generalize compared to DL pre-LLM, but it’s still nowhere near general enough for majority of human tasks especially in CS careers where a human in the loop will still be required for custom solutions. So don’t bogged down by the hype.
 Twitter post Blog post
 Highlighting the most relevant bits:
  Andrew Ng @AndrewYNg I recently received an email titled “An 18-year-old’s dilemma: Too late to contribute to AI?” Its author, who gave me permission to share this, is preparing for college. He is worried that by the time he graduates, AI will be so good there’s no meaningful work left for him to do to contribute to humanity, and he will just live on Universal Basic Income (UBI). I wrote back to reassure him that there will still be plenty of work he can do for decades hence, and encouraged him to work hard and learn to build with AI. But this conversation struck me as an example of how harmful hype about AI is. […] Even though LLMs can handle a much more general set of tasks than previous iterations of AI technology, compared to what humans can do, they are still highly specialized. They’re much better at working with text than other modalities, still require lots of custom engineering to get it the right context for a particular application, and we have few tools — and only inefficient ones — for getting our systems to learn from feedback and repeated exposure to a specific task (such as screening resumés for a particular role). […] AI has stark limitations, and despite rapid improvements, it will remain limited compared to humans for a long time. […] Modern AI is a general purpose technology that is enabling many applications, but AI that can do any intellectual tasks that a human can (a popular definition for AGI) is still decades away or longer. This nuanced message that AI is general, but not that general, often is lost in the noise of today's media environment. […] Similarly, the progress of frontier models is amazing! But not so amazing that they’ll be able to do everything under the sun without a lot of customization. I know VC investors who are scared to invest in application-layer startups because they are worried that frontier AI model companies will quickly wipe out all of these businesses by improving their models. While some thin wrappers around LLMs no doubt will be replaced, there also remains a huge set of valuable applications that the current trajectory of progress of frontier models won’t displace for a long time.

text:
Completed Airbnb's Staff+ loop - here are my thoughts

EDIT: Removed the links to the tagged questions since many people seem hung up on this being a potential ad. I understand, we're all tired of ads. Now back to the aim of this post, providing clarity on the process.
 Summary
 I just completed Airbnb's Staff+ loop recently and I want to share some thoughts about the process, the timeline, my preparation strategy and feelings about the future as I wait for the result.
 Background
 I have interviewed with Airbnb for a senior role about five years ago and bombed so bad in the very first round that it made me question my choice of career.
 This time, a sr recruiter reached out to me on LinkedIn in July and I formally started the interview process soon after that. I believe Airbnb changed its loop structure (not sure if it's for all levels or for staff+ only) during this time so there was some churn on the interview structure as I was going through it.
 Process
 We scheduled a quick phone call to go over the process that looks like this at a high level:
   Round Format Notes    HM Screen (1x) 60 minutes; a mid-level conversation about my work ex., preferred areas of work, team's area of work, short to mid term challenges the team faces etc. It is my belief that beyond helping Airbnb decide if they should spend time interviewing me, it also helps decide the level I should continue interviewing for.   Architecture (2x) 60 minutes; 1 system design problem, few follow up questions on scaling, edge cases, CAP theorem tradeoffs etc. What I found most interesting was that they turned out to be super engaging conversations between two staff+ engineers about interesting edge cases in the given problem and clever optimizations one could add. The actual diagramming I did was super minimal and I was told not to worry about it since the conversation is going in the "right" direction.   Experience Interview (1x) 60 minutes; a low-level conversation with a staff+ engineer about my work experience in general and up to two long-running, large-scale projects specifically. I always have two slide decks (with diagrams) lying around to explain two of my recent/favorite projects. It also helps that one of the large features I've shipped is publicly used by about 2 billion MAUs so I use that as a "live" demo, too! The conversation then went deep into all the real-life sharding issues, and operational concerns one deals with at that scale.   Coding (1x) 45 minutes; a heavily modified version of a popular problem tagged to Airbnb. I was able to quickly solve the problem, clear the edge cases and get it to run. We spent the rest of the time optimizing it for runtime and discussed how something like this could be deployed in production.   Core Values (x1) 60 minutes; a behavioral round seen through the lens of Airbnb's core values. This turned out to be more deep and personal than any interview I've taken or given. Very interesting!   Timeline
 I had a great time managing the timeline for this loop. I really appreciated the level of flexibility Airbnb offers candidates. You get your own portal where you can track and manage your interview process with them. You can request reschedules (latest by an hour before the interview) and push interviews away as far as you need.
 Preparation Strategy
 Preparing for this loop felt really smooth compared to some of the loops I've given before. Something that really helped this time around was the sheer of volume of interviews I've conducted on behalf of my current employer. I got really used to the process, its stated claims, and ways to optimize those 60 minutes from one side of the desk, that it made the other side very approachable.
 I did not prepare for my architecture interviews at all. One of my unpopular opinions is that any staff+ engineer should be able to give an architecture interview in a moment's notice. It's very simply a narrow application of something you ought to be doing everyday at work, at least ideally.
 I always go back to this video by Jackson Gabbard as my foundation for preparing for behavioral interviews and this time was no different.
 For the coding rounds, I focused on the Airbnb tagged questions. This was very helpful.
 I would also recommend this sequence of processing coding problems as it really helped me:
  Verbally explain the naive solution (e.g. to pick the Kth largest element, we could simply sort this array and pick the Kth element from the end) and why you wouldn't want to implement that.
 Write down your proposed solution as a multi-line code comment. If possible, outline possible edge cases or rooms for optimization right away.
 Write down the key steps of your algorithm as single line code comments and get buy-in.

text:
I joined Google and I’m really disappointed

Before I start, I just want to make it clear that yes I am grateful for my job. I do know that the tech industry has so many layoffs right now and many people would do a lot to be in my position. This is not a lack of gratitude, it’s me sharing sincere feelings with the hope that I can get over them. 
 Google is probably a dream company for many people. It certainly was for me. For context, I’ve worked at 3 tech companies before, one of which was big tech. I’m in a slightly technical program management role, mid-career, and have been good at delivering in the roles I’ve been in. I’ve always (for the 10yrs of my entire career) wanted to work for Google. I’d always assumed it had the smartest people in the industry that were kind, and had the best products in the industry, which meant the machine internally must have been very good. I’ve just passed probation and here’s what I’ve found:
  Let’s start with the confusing, uninspiring onboarding that took 2 weeks to just start. As in, I was given 2 weeks to set up my credentials (a 15mins call with the tech team that happened on my 2nd day). I didn’t know what to do with the rest of that time so I read up on random documents I could find. Eventually I was given an onboarding checklist with some broken links and some outdated docs as well. About a month later I received an invitation to the actual “Welcome to Google” orientation where I got to meet some other people who were also onboarding. Some of them had been waiting for this session for more than 2 months! We got a notebook and a pen during the session. Later received emails with different Noogler onboarding tracks. It honestly felt so disorganised and unthoughtful. Before you ask, I’ve met my manager, he’s a nice guy and all. But when I asked him things about the team, the role, the tools, an uncomfortable number of the answers were “don’t worry about that for now” which felt dwarfing to how eager I was to get orientated. 

 Most disappointingly, the people are not as smart and/or as rigorous as I’d imagined they were. I don’t mean offence to anyone, but some things really need to be called out. We have a guy in our team who needs to be told exactly what to do and how, otherwise he just malfunctions. I got the shock of my life when I showed him one of the documents he was working with had broken links we needed to update. He updated the one link we looked at and sent the document on with 5 other broken links. Surely an L4 should be able to get himself to look through a document and update it without further prompting? We have another who everyone complains about because of his attitude and inability to deliver work. His manager literally told me he is a difficult person to manage after I had an incident with him. And yet, he’s still here. And another guy who’s just incredibly aloof. The kind to run fix problems that don’t exist because he misread the doc on the problem he’s actually meant to be working on. And no, I’m not being hyper critical or petty, I can appreciate we all make mistakes, these are examples of patterns of lack of attention to detail, lack of initiative and overall very low standard of work. 

 What exacerbates the frustration above is how inflated these same people seem to be about just how smart and impactful they are. When you speak to some of these people, they can’t perform basic deductive reasoning (context: we are a data science adjacent team, not as technical, but analysis of insights is important), but the way they speak about themselves is incredible. They talk about how great the company is and how incompatible the perks are to everything else in the industry. As someone who’s been around the industry, it’s really not THAT great :-/ A lot of people here are highly tenured and I realised just how little they know about what’s going on outside the proverbial Google walls.

 Too many people fighting for relevance, but don’t have the creativity or experience to solve issues. When you spot a problem or gap, you’ll get told that it’s known and owned by someone, has been for months or in some cases years, but you don’t have to worry about collaborating with them to fix it. Even when the fix is super simple (again, experience in other companies gives you a problem solving arsenal) and your own work relies on the issue being fixed. The number of times I’ve pointed to a process and data that’s incorrect or inefficient and been told someone would get to it eventually is scary. 

 And why do the slides and documents look like that?? Like there are no designers or corporate branding folks here! Consistently the most cluttered, disorganised documents I’ve ever seen. I know the most important thing is the information but does everyone just not care about the presentation?? I attended a meeting for a VP which had different presenters from the team presenting different sections. I kid you not, each section had a different theme, look-and-feel, style, whatever you want to call it. In one deck for one meeting. To me, “best” in this case looks like one standardised deck that’s easy to read. Am I crazy for expecting that the “best” company in the world operates like this?

  Overall, it’s been a deeply disappointing few months. I honestly feel like this is where my ambition has come to die. So far nothing is as great as I thought it would be. Except maybe the food, but that’s not why I’m here. I’ve had the pleasure of working at companies like Facebook where I got to experience real ingenuity and the kind of people you want to have a corridor chats with because they really are wells of knowledge. Maybe my problem is that I’m seeking that thrill again and the area I’m in feels… stale. Or maybe I’ve just outgrown the level or role and I need to be honest with myself about that. 
 Of course I won’t leave. To do that would be like leaving earth because I think the government is ineffective. Just expressing some thoughts. Hoping to find some Googlers who can tell me that what I’m experiencing is unique to my org and there are other orgs that are… better.
